content.p: The Finks are an Australian outlaw motorcycle club. In October 2013 they became the centre of a major change of allegiance, when their members were reported to be crossing to the US-based Mongols. The Examiner called it a "bloodless takeover". After that, the Finks' name turned up in court cases and police raids in several states.

The cases described below involve assault, robbery, firearms and drugs. They also include a death in a Victorian prison that a coroner was examining in 2023. Where the accounts differ, the differences are given with the name of the person or outlet that made each claim.

In October 2013 the Examiner in Launceston reported that the Mongols had been "engaged in a bloodless takeover" of the Finks. The paper gave the scale as a "purported 90 per cent" of Finks members crossing to a club it described as known for its violent past. Speaking to the Herald Sun, the Mongols' new Melbourne chapter president said the public had nothing to fear and that there was no beef with any "one per cent" club.

The reasons were not settled. The Examiner wrote that the rationale "is not clear", but that internal tensions had been reported as one cause, along with the outlawing of the Finks in Queensland. In the week before, the paper said, 26 motorcycle clubs had been named as criminal organisations in Queensland, which forbade their members from associating with each other.

The Examiner reported that Tasmania Police confirmed the Finks were active in the state but had only a small membership and no clubhouse. Acting Assistant Police Commissioner Glen Frame said that anyone identified because of their criminal activity would be dealt with. The paper also reported that Queensland Supreme Court documents had described club members smuggling drugs through Launceston Airport.

In late November 2013 members of the Finks, wearing full colours, were spoken to by highway patrol officers in Ballarat, Victoria. The Courier reported that it was the first time the group had been seen in the town in more than two years. Police described the checks as routine and said some minor traffic infringements had been issued. The paper noted that the club had last been seen in the city in September 2011, when large numbers of members gathered in the central business district.

The Courier also reported at that time that members of the Finks nationwide were being "patched over" by the Mongols, which describes itself as the "baddest bikie gang in the world". The paper added that it had been reported that the Mongols were "enemies" of the Hells Angels.

The worst of the Ballarat incidents came in June 2014 at the Haida Bar on Camp Street. The Courier reported that police executed warrants at the Finks' central Ballarat clubhouse on a Monday morning, after staff and patrons at the nightclub were allegedly assaulted and the venue robbed shortly after midnight on the Saturday. Seven premises across the region were searched and three men were arrested. Superintendent Andrew Allen said police wanted to send a clear message: "We know that the Finks are trying to establish themselves up here". A June report placed the attack on the Saturday, while a September report gave the date as 5 June.

In September 2014 nine men appeared in Ballarat Magistrates Court for committal mention hearings. The Courier reported that two other men were due to face court over the alleged raid in November, and that three more were still at large. Each man faced offences including aggravated burglary, robbery, affray, intentionally and recklessly causing injury, and unlawful assault; the unlawful assault charges were five counts each. The committal hearing was set for ten days in February 2015 and was expected to hear from more than 20 witnesses, some of them patrons who were allegedly attacked. No plea is reported in the coverage.

A Taskforce Echo detective told the court that 15 Finks bikies, all in gang clothing, "forced" their way into the nightclub shortly after midnight. He said they assaulted a security guard, then staff and patrons, and stole cash from a register. They also threatened staff to turn off the CCTV cameras and tried to remove the cameras. He said the raid was planned and that Finks members travelled from Tasmania, Sydney, Adelaide and Melbourne to help the Ballarat members.

The detective put the group's presence in a wider context. "The Finks motorcycle club had all but died out in Australia," he said, adding: "There is evidence to suggest that they are trying to revamp themselves." He told the court there was "clear evidence that they're associated with criminal activity", and said that the group's presence, clothing and intimidation had been used "to intimidate people and then assault people".

In September 2023 two fully patched Finks members were sentenced in the Victorian County Court for an attack on a man at a factory in Dandenong. Joseph Muratore, 32, who had previously been a member of the Hells Angels, had pleaded guilty to recklessly causing serious injury by beating and stabbing the man on 6 March 2022. Lee Martin, 48, who had joined the Finks in his forties, had been charged with assault on the basis of complicity and with refusing to give police access to his phone.

The court heard that the two men and a senior Finks member, John Pahoumidis, boxed in the man's car in the factory driveway. Pahoumidis punched him in the jaw. When he tried to run, Muratore threw a metal stand at his head, then kicked him in the torso and tackled him to the ground, where he beat and stabbed him. A bystander found him bleeding on the nature strip and got him medical help. Judge Liz Gaynor told Muratore: "If he had died you would have been facing a charge of murder."

Muratore received a sentence of three years and four months, with 20 months to serve before he could be considered for parole. Martin was sentenced to time already served, which was 15 months. Pahoumidis had pleaded guilty to assault and drug possession and was due to be sentenced the following March. Judge Gaynor described the men's involvement with the club as "pathetic" and "the grossest immaturity", and said Muratore was "not 15" but "a man in his 30s".

In November 2025 police in the Hunter region of New South Wales linked two weekends of violence to the Finks. The incidents included pub brawls at Merewether and Shoal Bay and an alleged knife threat to a patron. A 25-year-old woman claimed that an unknown man had touched her on three occasions at a Merewether pub on 1 November. That night, a 28-year-old man was allegedly involved in a brawl in which he armed himself with a knife and threatened a patron. The following weekend, at the Shoal Bay Country Club, men allegedly attacked patrons standing outside, and one man was alleged to have punched a patron to the ground.

Raptor Squad North, a unit of the State Crime Command, launched seven searches in Lake Macquarie, Cessnock and Maitland. The haul included guns, drugs and money, and officers arrested eight alleged members and associates of the Finks, as well as the partner of one of the men. Police refused bail to four of those charged. One man was charged with 10 firearm offences after a 12-gauge shotgun was found hidden in a couch. His partner pleaded guilty to three firearm offences and was granted bail; her solicitor said the shotgun had been brought into the house "against her will".
Police said the men were members and associates of the Finks. These are police allegations at the bail stage; no plea is reported for most of those arrested.
content.h2: The ACT Rebels and the Finks
content.p: A bail hearing in Canberra in April 2025 shed light on how a rival club had been absorbed. Police told the court that the ACT Rebels had "disbanded" and become the "All Brothers Crew" between late 2022 and early 2023, and that its members had then "patched over" to the Finks in 2023. A detective alleged that a man in his fifties had been president of the Canberra Rebels and was now believed by police to be a "world president" of the Finks. A detective said police intelligence suggested that a person a prominent Canberra lawyer had identified as president of the ACT Finks was a "figurehead" and not actually in charge.

The man before the court faced 11 family violence charges and had pleaded not guilty to all of them: two counts of choking, eight counts of assault and one of unlawful confinement. A magistrate granted him bail on 16 April. The ACT Director of Public Prosecutions appealed, and the ACT Supreme Court reviewed the decision the next day. Justice David Mossop refused bail. He said he was satisfied the man had stayed in touch with the Finks, and that this was unlikely to have stopped. A second detective told the court that prosecutions of motorcycle club members rarely relied on witness statements because of the gangs' reputations, and that a person who gave evidence against a member "will be at extreme risk".
content.h2: Death of Brent Reker in custody
content.p: Brent Reker, described in a 2023 report as a Finks boss, died at Ravenhall prison in Victoria on 12 December 2019. He was 35 and on remand for violent drug and weapon offences. He had been moved from Port Phillip Prison into a specialist mental health unit at Ravenhall in November 2019, after earlier attempts to take his own life.

About three weeks later, staff became concerned that he was influencing other prisoners in the unit through comments he made about self-harm. Counsel assisting the coroner, Leading Senior Constable Fiona Nation, said staff had agreed he was at risk of influencing the group. A psychiatrist was supposed to speak to him before he was moved but did not, because the clinician had already left the unit. At about 2.30pm on 12 December, officers began moving him. He was argumentative and animated when told. A psychiatrist sent to his new cell at about 3.30pm got no response, and the cell door was blocked by a mattress. Prison officers then called a "code black" medical emergency, and he was found unconscious on the floor of the shower at 3.38pm.

In March 2023 Coroner Paul Lawrie was examining the events leading to the move, Reker's mental health history and the risk assessment carried out by staff. He was also examining how Corrections Victoria answered the recommendations of a 2021 justice system review. The 2023 report said the coroner was investigating whether the move contributed to Reker taking his own life.
